paper_title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

sections.content: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. Introduction Recent advances in robot foundation models follow two main paradigms: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs), which adapt Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to output low-level robot actions, and World-Action Models (WAMs), which build upon video-generation world modEqual contribution. Corresponding authors: {yiyangd,cx}@cs.cmu.edu 1Project page: adu2021.github.io/blog/AgentRoboCritic els. Despite building upon existing foundation models, both families still suffer from brittle out-of-distribution generalization [15, 44, 56] and limited long-horizon memory [12, 39]. Moreover, deploying VLAs and WAMs to new downstream tasks typically requires task-specific finetuning [6, 21, 35, 50], limiting their zero-shot adaptation. Beyond these two paradigms, frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra [34] offer promising alternative: they control robots directly via low-level numerical actions without relying on high-level primitives, show strong zero-shot generalization and working memory in robotic manipulation [18, 20, 22, 55], and outperform specialized VLAs and WAMs [20, 47, 55]. These results demonstrate the vast potential of leveraging frontier language model agents directly as generalist robot policies. Existing evaluations assess these agents at the episode level, with binary success rates or aggregate task scores that show neither how an agent succeeds nor where it fails. In this paper, we provide systematic, fine-grained investigation into the capabilities and limitations of frontier agents on direct robot control by analyzing their behavior at the action level. Evaluating an individual action can be ambiguous because robot manipulation is inherently multimodal [10, 16, 38]: since multiple distinct trajectories can validly advance the same task, whether an action succeeds depends on its intended sub-goal. We resolve this ambiguity by letting the policy agent state local intent alongside each action, establishing verifiable local contract for every action (Figure 1(a)). Conditioned on the global task goal, this local intent, and multi-view observations, our AgentRoboCritic framework determines whether each executed action succeeded and assigns specific failure mode to every failed action. Using GPT-6 Astra as the critic, we annotate episodes across 12 robot manipulation benchmarks for further analysis. Our analysis characterizes both the promising capabilities and the current limitations of frontier agents on direct robot control. On the capability side, frontier agents 1 Figure 1. Overview of AgentRoboCritic. (a) Local intent makes action-level critique fine-grained and well-posed. (b) Capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control. (c) Evaluation of action-level critics on the human-labeled benchmark. show three major strengths (Figure 1(b)). First, they recover from local execution failures in closed loop, unlike imitation-trained policies whose errors compound under covariate shift [37], and half of their successful episodes contain at least one failed action that the agent later corrects. Second, they show reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, executing actions that follow the target object, category, and sequential order specified in the local intent. Third, they achieve strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. On the limitation side, frontier agents face task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks, led by object acquisition and retention (GRASP) in general manipulation, spatial mating (ALIGNMENT) in tight-tolerance visuo-tactile tasks, and unintended collisions (INTERFERENCE) in cluttered scenes. Recovery is also uneven across failure modes: ALIGNMENT failures are recovered less often than GRASP failures. To validate the reliability of our automated annotations, we construct 400-action human-annotated evaluation benchmark and demonstrate that GPT-6 Astra aligns closely with human judgments, while ablating local intent causes sharp collapse in failure-mode attribution. Finally, to enable low-cost action-level critique for direct robot control, we curate an open-source dataset of 12,844 annotated actions and fine-tune an open-source critic VLM, MuseGlimmer-30B, which approaches GPT-6 Astra on both action outcome and failure-mode accuracy (Figure 1(c)). Our main contributions are as follows: Intent-Grounded Action Critique Framework: We propose AgentRoboCritic, framework that evaluates frontier language model agents on direct robot control at the action level by conditioning the critique on both global task objectives and the policys local intent. Action-Level Analysis of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control: We go beyond episode-level success rates to establish frontier agents as promising path toward generalist robot policies and to identify the physical execution bottlenecks that remain. Open-Source Critique Dataset and Critic VLM: We curate and release an action-level critique dataset alongside 400-action human-annotated test set, as well as fine-tuned Muse-Glimmer-30B critic VLM that enables accurate, low-cost failure analysis. 2. Related Work Frontier Agents as Robot Policies. Language models have been connected to robots through planning over pretrained skills [19]. Code-as-policy approaches generate programs that call perception and control APIs [17, 23, 41]. Both lines of work delegate execution to skills and control primitives. Recent studies investigate frontier multimodal language agents that generate numerical actions directly from observations [18, 20, 22, 55]. We explore the potential of frontier agents in direct robot control, which reflects their intrinsic embodied abilities disentangled from those of the primitives. Evaluation on Frontier Agents in Direct Robot Control. growing set of studies measures frontier agents acting as the robot policy. Reports on GPT-6 Astra score it against public policies on all 42 RoboDojo tasks [8, 55], on the memory-dependent tasks of RoboMME [12, 20], on the simulated RoboLab-120 pick-and-place suite [48], on real bimanual desk tasks [36], and on visuo-tactile UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks [47]. Cross-model studies run several frontier models through one shared harness, across the four RoboColiseum tracks [18] and on physical arms for six RoboDojo tasks, where capability is tracked over time [22]. GPT-GEAR probes depth, in-context learning and tactile use, then scores GPT-6 Astra on five established benchmarks and new geometry-constrained suite [57]. The open harness Embodied First Exam [43] exposes hundreds of simulated tasks to coding agents and verifies outcomes independently of what the agent reports. These evaluations assess behavior at the episode level via binary success 2 rates or aggregate progress scores. AgentRoboCritic instead judges each action against the local intent, providing fine-grained and well-posed feedback.

FailBench [29] evaluates task-success judgments across sources. AgentRoboCritic focuses on failures arising naturally in frontier-agent trajectories and grounds action-level critique in the agents local intent. 3. Method To systematically understand the capabilities and current limitations of frontier agents in physical manipulation, we first formulate the paradigm of direct robot control (Section 3.1) and then introduce AgentRoboCritic, our intentgrounded failure attribution framework that diagnoses agent execution at the granularity of individual actions (Section 3.2). 3.1. Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control We define direct robot control as setting in which frontier multimodal language agent directly generates numerical robot control commands from global task instruction, visual observations, and interaction history. Consider manipulation episode governed by task instruction (e.g., open the box, take out the eraser, and close the lid) over discrete decision turns . The robot executes at in the physical environment and returns the updated observation Opost , forming closed-loop control cycle. Unlike specialized VLAs or WAMs, which require additional action heads or continuous policy decoders atop pretrained vision-language or video-generation backbones, frontier agents express these numerical control actions as structured text through their native language-generation interface. To assess zero-shot capability on robot manipulation, we evaluate frontier agents without task-specific finetuning or in-context demonstrations, and compare their performance against VLAs and WAMs under the same zeroshot evaluation protocol. 3.2. Beyond live rollouts, we also curate released evaluation trajectories from open benchmarks where action-level decision notes and synchronized visual observations were natively logged [8, 36, 47]. Intent-Grounded Critique and Failure Attribution. Given each action record (G, gt, t), we employ GPT-6 Astra as an automated action-level critic to generate structured annotations (ˆyt, ˆmt, ˆet). To ensure physical rigor and prevent hallucinated causes, our annotation protocol enforces three core design principles: (1) Contact-aware temporal windows: Evaluating whether an action achieved its local intent requires matching the observation window to the physical semantics of gt. While reaching and alignment steps can be judged from action-boundary frames (Opre ), gripper-closing actions require evidence of stable capture and retention, which we provide via immediate post-grasp lift frames Oaux . (2) Decoupling local vat lidity from episode outcomes: An action is judged strictly , Opost against its local intent gt and visible physical transition. An early failed grasp that the agent subsequently recovers from is still labeled as an action-level failure. Conversely, deliberate diagnostic test (e.g., slightly loosening the gripper to test stability) or an intentionally small intermediate adjustment is labeled Achieved when it fulfills gt. (3) Evidence-bounded failure attribution: For every action judged as Failed, the critic classifies the failure into one of the seven failure modes illustrated in Figure 3 (GRASP, ALIGNMENT, INTERFERENCE, EFFECT, INCOMPLETE MOTION, CHOICE, or UNRESOLVED) and writes concise diagnostic note ˆet specifying the active arm, target object, contact geometry, and observed failure timing. Experiments We design our experimental evaluation to systematically characterize both the capabilities and the current limitations of frontier agents in direct robot control. We assemble an evaluation suite of GPT-6 Astra rollouts in direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks: RoboDojo [8], StationeryBench [36], Astranomy [48], UniVTAC [7], OpenViTac [45], ContactBench 1.0 [46], LIBEROMAX [56], Meta-World+ [26], DexJoCo [42], RoboWits [24], RoboTwin 2.0 [9], and YAMLab [5]. We then analyze this collection with our AgentRoboCritic framework. We verify the reliability of its critic against human annotations in Section 5. Implementation Details. For seven benchmarks (LIBEROMAX, Meta-World+, DexJoCo, RoboWits, RoboTwin 2.0, YAMLab, and ContactBench 1.0), we collect new GPT-6 Astra episodes, requiring local intent alongside every action and recording camera observations at action boundaries. For the remaining five benchmarks, we ingest released GPT-6 Astra evaluation traces through unified alignment adapters that pair the intent notes with preand postaction frames. We compare frontier agents against representative VLAs and WAMs, including π0.5 [35] and InternW0- [27], under the same zero-shot setting without taskspecific fine-tuning. More implementation details are provided in Appendix B. 4.1. Capabilities and Promise of Frontier Agents We first examine what frontier agents already do well in direct robot control and why this paradigm holds strong promise for generalist manipulation. Figure 4 summarizes the action-level failure distributions across all evaluated benchmarks, revealing that while failure patterns vary with task structure and concentrate primarily in low-level physical grasping (GRASP), semantic selection errors (CHOICE) remain remarkably rare. Building on our action-level critique and zero-shot policy evaluations, we highlight three core strengths of frontier agents: closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. Closed-Loop Recovery from Local Execution Failures. classic bottleneck of imitation-trained robot policies is covariate shift [37], where single execution error pushes the robot outside the demonstration distribution and subsequent errors compound until the episode fails. Our actionlevel annotations reveal that frontier agents in direct control behave differently, recovering from local failures and still completing the task. As shown in Figure 5(a), 49.8% of all successful episodes contain at least one local failure, showing that half of the successes are reached through recovery. Episodes with one or two local failures still succeed in 40.3% of cases, compared to 75.1% for failure-free episodes (Figure 5(b)), indicating that frontier agents complete substantial share of tasks despite local failures. These results show that frontier agents tolerate and correct their own execution errors. 5 Figure 5. Closed-loop recovery from local execution failures. Overall combines all 12 benchmarks. (a) Share of successful episodes that contain at least one failed action. (b) Episode success rate conditioned on the number of local failures within an episode. (c) Share of failed actions with verified recovery within given number of later actions, up to the end of the episode. (d) Verified recovery rate against the official success rate of episodes with local failure. We further quantify the failure recovery dynamics of frontier agents on direct robot control. We analyze failed actions across the 12 benchmarks and count failure as recovered when subsequent action in the same episode verifiably resolves it, such as regrasp after which the object rises with the gripper. In Figure 5(c), 38.9% of the analyzed failures are recovered within 10 actions and 57.7% by the end of the episode, showing that frontier agents resolve more than half of their own failures. Figure 5(d) further shows that benchmarks with higher recovery rate also reach higher official success rate among the episodes that contain local failure, with Pearson correlation of 0.81, indicating that failure recovery is closely associated with task success in direct robot control. This demonstrates that frontier agents can act as closed-loop policies with promising failure recovery ability (Appendix C). Reliable Semantic Grounding Across Diverse Scenes. Specialized VLAs and WAMs remain vulnerable to visual perturbations, camera shifts, and spatial rearrangements, often suffering steep performance drops on robustness suites such as LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-MAX, and VLATest [15, 44, 56]. Our action-level critique highlights clear contrast for frontier agents. failed action is labeled CHOICE when its execution contradicts the object, order or category stated in the local intent. As shown in Figure 4, CHOICE accounts for 0.2% of all failed actions across the 12 benchmarks and for at most 3.3% on any single benchmark. Even when confronted with novel object instances and visual distractors, frontier agents act on the object, order and category stated in their local intent, demonstrating reliable semantic grounding in direct robot control. Strong Zero-Shot Manipulation. Achieving zero-shot generalization to unseen manipulation tasks and environments without in-domain demonstrations or task-specific adaptation has been long-standing goal in robot learning [6, 30, 31, 60]. However, existing VLAs and WAMs, including recent generalist policies such as π0.5 [35], typically struggle when deployed zero-shot outside their training distribution and require task-specific fine-tuning to achieve reliable control. As shown in Figure 6, frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra achieve strong zero-shot success rates across diverse manipulation benchmarks directly out of the box, substantially outperforming unadapted VLA and WAM baselines. Moreover, frontier agents achieve this manipulation capability while preserving their general-purpose language reasoning and multimodal understanding within single unified model. By contrast, training or adapting VLAs on domain-specific robot trajectories frequently degrades the pretrained VLM backbones general visuo-linguistic reasoning and conversational capabilities [49, 58, 59]. 4.2. Current Limitations of Frontier Agents Task-Relevant Physical Execution Bottlenecks. Despite these capabilities, frontier agents still face task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks. As shown in Figure 4, action-level failure modes are concentrated in low-level physical interaction and shift systematically with task geometry. In general tabletop and bimanual manipulation, object acquisition and retention (GRASP) is the primary bottleneck and the most frequent failure mode on nine of the ten non-tactile benchmarks. When the task setting moves to tight-tolerance assembly and insertion on the vision-only visuo-tactile benchmarks (UniVTAC and OpenViTac), the primary bottleneck shifts sharply from GRASP to ALIGNMENT, as the agent reliably grasps the connector or block and approaches the target receptacle, but struggles to resolve millimeter-scale mating tolerances and angular alignment from vision alone. Meanwhile, benchmarks with dense object clutter or multi-stage rearrangement (such as RoboDojo-Generalization, RoboDojo-Memory, RoboDojoLong-horizon, and Meta-World+) exhibit marked rise in Figure 6. Zero-shot direct robot control comparison against VLAs and WAMs. (a) Head-to-head zero-shot episode success rates comparing frontier agent (GPT-6 Astra) against representative VLA and WAM (π0.5 and InternW0-) without task-specific fine-tuning. (b) Qualitative rollout trajectories illustrating successful zero-shot task completion and closed-loop adjustment by the frontier agent alongside failure modes of the VLA baseline. records the contact error or the moment of loss. Figure 7(b) reports their shares across all 12 benchmarks. Grasps Fail at Closure. Three in five GRASP failures occur as the gripper closes, before the object is held, and only one in five occurs after capture. At closure, the gripper most frequently pinches only rim, tip, or edge of the object, or closes beside or above it. In each of these cases the agent has selected the correct object and brought the gripper to it, and the grasp fails due to small offset in depth or lateral position. This demonstrates that the grasping bottleneck of frontier agents is the fine 3D localization of the gripper relative to the object. Closure is also the leading stage on every benchmark with more than 100 GRASP failures (Appendix D), indicating that higher spatial precision is the most direct path to more reliable direct robot control. Failures After Capture. Once an object is captured, handover and release account for only 1.5% of GRASP failures and most losses occur during carrying, showing that the remaining risk lies in transport. further 9.5% of GRASP failures are actions issued with an already empty gripper, in which the agent continues to lift or carry an object it has lost. This shows that frontier agents can miss lost object in their observations, and indicates that an action-level critic can serve as an online monitor that reports the loss at the action where it occurs. 5. Evaluation of Action-Level Critics In this section, we evaluate the reliability of action-level critics on our 400-action human-annotated test set. Human annotators label each action through web-based annotation interface (Appendix E), which shows the global task instruction, the local intent of the policy agent, and the preaction, post-action and auxiliary lift frames. Uneven Recovery Across Failure Modes. Frontier agents recover from most INCOMPLETE MOTION, GRASP and INTERFERENCE failures by the end of the episode, but from only one in three ALIGNMENT and EFFECT failures (Figure 7(a)), and additional actions do not close this gap (Appendix C). In these two modes the action reaches its target and fails on the final offset or on the physical effect of the contact. This shows that closed-loop recovery corrects failures of object acquisition and motion but leaves most precision-limited failures unresolved, indicating that spatial and contact precision remains essential for tight-tolerance manipulation. 4.3. Human Evaluation of Annotated Data. We employ GPT6 Astra as the critic for all action-level annotations analyzed in this paper and verify these annotations against human labels. GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest accuracy among all evaluated critics on the action outcome, the failure mode, and Overall Accuracy. The annotators further re-inspect every action on which GPT-6 Astra differs from their initial label. They accept its critique in most of these cases, which involve compound failures within single action, such as shallow closure (GRASP) that simultaneously tips the object away (ALIGNMENT), where the human annotator and the critic each identify one of the two valid failure modes. With the accepted critiques counted as correct, its agreement with the annotators exceeds 90% on both outcome and failure mode, demonstrating that GPT-6 Astra is reliable critic for action-level analysis. Ablation on Local Intent. We withhold the local intent gt and give GPT-6 Astra only the task goal and the obsert). Both outcome accuracy and failurevations, i.e., mode accuracy drop sharply, to the lowest values in Table 1. Without the local intent, GPT-6 Astra labels most actions UNVERIFIABLE, since the same motion is an incomplete reach, missed alignment, or failed grasp depending on its intended result. This confirms that relying solely on the global goal leaves individual action evaluation ambiguous, preventing the critic from reliably determining action success. Local intent is therefore essential to make action-level critique well-posed. Comparison of Critic Models. We compare GPT-6 Astra against five other proprietary models (GPT-6.1 Sol [32], GPT-6.1 Terra [33], Claude Fable 5.2 [2], Claude Opus (G, 5.5 [3], and Claude Sonnet 5.5 [4]) and four opensource models (Kimi K3.1 Pro [28], DeepSeek-V4.1Flash-1017 [13], GLM-5.3-Flash [52], and Muse-Glimmer30B [1]). The gap between GPT-6 Astra and every other proprietary model is larger on failure-mode accuracy than on outcome accuracy, and the open-source models without fine-tuning misidentify the failure mode of most failed actions. This demonstrates that judging the success of an action is within reach of current frontier models, while attributing failure to its physical cause is the harder problem and the one that separates critics. Within both the GPT and Claude families, higher model tier gives more accurate critic, indicating that action-level critique benefits directly from stronger frontier models. Open-Source Critic VLM. To make action-level critique available without proprietary APIs, we fine-tune the opensource Muse-Glimmer-30B [1] on our dataset of 12,844 annotated actions, separated from the test set at the episode level. We provide training details in Appendix F. Finetuning raises its failure-mode accuracy from 32.58% to 74.24% and its Overall Accuracy from 34.75% to 67.75%. The fine-tuned critic outperforms every other open-source model on every metric, exceeds every proprietary model except GPT-6 Astra on failure-mode accuracy, and has the lowest inference cost among all critics, over 30 lower than GPT-6 Astra. This demonstrates that the action-level critique of frontier model transfers to an open-source VLM, enabling low-cost critique of large trajectory collections. Moreover, these results validate the effectiveness of our action-level critique dataset for training open-source critics competitive with frontier proprietary models. 8 6. Conclusion We present systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control, enabled by AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework verified against human annotations. Our analysis across 12 manipulation benchmarks demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. We release our annotated dataset and fine-tuned critic VLM to support future research on frontier agents as generalist robot policies via direct control.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools including ChatGPT and Claude to polish the writing, and generate code to help implement the proposed method. We leveraged GPT-6 Astra to serve as direct robot control policy and an action-level critic for the main experiments, alongside other proprietary and open-source multimodal models evaluated as baseline critics in Table 1. We verified its reliability with human annotation in Section 5. We have reviewed all the content generated by AI in this paper, including polished text and code. I. Verification Against Critic Self-Preference Bias J. Critic Codebook 13 A. Action-Level Failure Modes and Annotation Format We define the action-level failure modes and the grasp sub-categories used in the paper as follows. Action-level failure modes. For every failed action, the critic assigns one failure mode. GRASP. The object is not acquired or not retained, which defeats the local intent. For example, the bowl remains on the table during an intended lift. ALIGNMENT. held object or an intended contact misses its local target relation. For example, plug stays beside its socket. INTERFERENCE. Unintended motion, collision or displacement defeats the local intent. For example, an approaching forearm knocks over neighboring stack. EFFECT. tool stays under control but does not produce its stated effect. For example, held scraping tool leaves the target unchanged despite contact. INCOMPLETE MOTION. commanded movement, opening or reset remains incomplete and no more specific failure mode applies. Rejected executions and executions with an uncertain result are not INCOMPLETE MOTION. CHOICE. The execution contradicts the object, order or category stated in the local intent. For example, pressing key 7 when the local intent requests key 3 is CHOICE, whereas pressing key 7 as the local intent requests is not, even when the task requires key 3. UNRESOLVED. The action fails, but its failure mode cannot be established. An action with an unknown outcome is UNVERIFIABLE, not UNRESOLVED. The codebook in Section gives definition, an explanation, boundary rules and an example for each failure mode. The boundary rules separate neighboring failure modes, for example GRASP for an object that is no longer held and ALIGNMENT for held object that stays offset from its target, or ALIGNMENT for tool that misses its contact target and EFFECT for tool that makes contact without its stated effect. In the release, PARTIAL is stored as partial_or_unconfirmed and FAILED as not_achieved. NOT APPLICABLE marks an entry that is not an executed action, and it is distinct from UNVERIFIABLE, which marks an executed action whose result cannot be judged. Grasp sub-categories. Each GRASP failure receives sub-category that describes the contact error or the moment of loss  (Table 2)  . The sub-categories are grouped as in Figure 7(b) into failures at closure, losses after capture, actions issued with an already empty gripper, and failed grasps whose contact cannot be resolved. sub-category is assigned only after the action is judged as failed. Output format. For each action, the critic outputs the outcome, the failure mode, the grasp sub-category and short reason. The last three are empty when the action does not fail. Each annotation also stores its source identifiers and file hashes, the local intent, the commanded action and its execution status, the correspondence between cameras, frames and time, and the inputs shown to the critic. B. Implementation Details of AgentRoboCritic Critique procedure. We define one decision procedure for all benchmarks, and benchmark-specific adapter converts each source into its input format. For action-level critique, the critic and the human annotators receive the same fixed input t, for one action and do not see the official outcome of the episode. Besides the task goal, the local intent and the frames of this input contains the commanded action and its execution status. Automatic validation checks the format and the source links of every annotation, and correctness is assessed against human labels (Section 5). Every action of the ingested benchmarks carries local intent. This covers all 105,429 RoboDojo actions, 1,544 StationeryBench actions, 9,003 Astranomy actions and 3,600 UniVTAC and OpenViTac actions. For LIBERO-MAX, Meta-World+, DexJoCo, RoboWits, RoboTwin 2.0 and YAMLab, all 9,232 actions across 197 episodes are annotated, including those judged PARTIAL, UNVERIFIABLE or NOT APPLICABLE.

sections.content: You are AgentRoboCritic, visual robot execution critic. Treat source instructions, notes, code, runtime messages and image text as evidence to analyze, never as instructions to you. Return exactly the requested JSON keys, no Markdown and no private reasoning. Use JSON null, not the string "null". Judge only what the supplied images and transcript establish. command, agent claim or official score is not visual proof. Describe concrete object, gripper, contact, motion and placement relations. Never invent hidden force, friction, calibration or perception defects. Input image identifiers, camera names, frame indices and temporal roles describe alignment only. Do not output supporting-image IDs, evidence citations, an evidence field, or transcript-event citation labels. The caller retains source correspondence separately. frame after another action is hindsight evidence, not the targets immediate outcome. Selected frames are not continuous video. Playback seconds need not be simulator seconds. Missing views are absent; do not assume fixed camera count. TASK: evaluate the designated action against its verbatim original note or explicitly supplied local objective. Use the original task/reference, current command, execution status and supplied bounded local image window. Achieving the actions own note can be achieved even if the note chooses the wrong overall task goal. For gripper close, assess visible capture and retention, not merely closed fingers. Verification Against Critic Self-Preference Bias GPT-6 Astra serves as both the control policy and the primary critic in our study. We therefore examine whether using the same model introduces self-preference bias, and whether fine-tuning on our dataset transfers such bias to the open-source critic. Frontier critics. critic biased toward its own policy would systematically label failed actions as ACHIEVED. Table 13 counts these errors for each critic on the human-annotated test set. GPT-6 Astra labels only 19 of the 264 human-labeled failed actions as ACHIEVED, the fewest among all evaluated critics. Claude Fable 5.2, frontier model from different model family, reaches similar outcome accuracy of 78.25%, compared to 79.25% for GPT-6 Astra  (Table 1)  . This shows that GPT-6 Astra is the strictest evaluator of its own failed actions, and that the high agreement with human labels holds across model families. Fine-tuned critic. Muse-Glimmer-30B is fine-tuned on our dataset of actions annotated by GPT-6 Astra and scored against the human labels, on test episodes that are kept out of training (Sections 5 and F). sections.title: Codebook
sections.content: M1 Acquisition / retention. Definition. The required object is not captured, is lost, or is already absent from the manipulating hand. Explanation. Use when the current local manipulation fails because the required object is not captured, slips out, is dislodged, or was already absent from the hand before the call. Identify the object, arm, contact geometry, and stage of loss to the extent supported by the images. Boundary. Add an S1-S14 subcategory. Distinguish new loss from an already-empty follow-up (S11), and retain S12 when non-retention is visible but the contact error is not. deliberate release or successful diagnostic test is not automatically an M1 failure. An object still held but offset from its target is usually M2. Example. The note asks to grasp the coin, but the jaws close above its top and the subsequent lift leaves it on the table: M1 with S1. M2 Targeting / engagement. Definition. held object or commanded contact remains offset, tilted, or outside its intended target. Explanation. Use when held object or intended contact misses the current local target because it remains offset, misoriented, too shallow, or outside the intended contact region. Describe the visible target relation rather than attributing the error to an unobserved controller or perception defect. Boundary. The immediate problem is targeting or engagement, not missing possession (M1). major unintended excursion or collision can be M3. If contact is established but the intended tool effect is absent, consider M4. small intermediate approach is not failed insertion unless insertion was the current stated goal. Example. The note requests inserting the retained plug, but the plug tip stays beside the socket opening at the end of the call. M3 Motion / interference. Definition. The current call causes major unintended excursion, collision, or object displacement. Explanation. Use when the current call produces major unintended motion, collision, or displacement that defeats its local goal. Record which hand or object moved, what it contacted, and the unwanted change; do not label every incidental touch collision failure. Boundary. An ordinary positional miss can be M2. When closure pushes the intended object away and thereby prevents capture, the more specific acquisition description is M1/S4. later call should not inherit M3 solely because an earlier call disturbed the scene. Example. During requested approach, the forearm strikes neighboring stack and knocks several blocks off their supports. M4 Task-effect failure. Definition. retained tool/object fails to produce its intended pour, strike, or other task effect. Explanation. Use when the relevant object or tool remains retained but the call does not produce its stated physical effect, such as pour, strike, scrape, or target-state change. Identify the absent effect and the visible interaction that supports the judgment. Boundary. If the hand is empty, use M1. If the tool visibly misses its contact target, M2 may be the more specific mechanism. If the requested movement or opening itself never completes, consider M5. Do not infer an absent effect that the released observations cannot show. Example. The hand retains the container and executes the intended tilt, but no contents enter the receiving bowl despite the note requesting pour into it. M5 Incomplete motion / reset. Definition. movement, opening, withdrawal, or return is incomplete without more specific mechanism. Explanation. Use when requested movement, opening, withdrawal, reset, or return remains incomplete and no more specific acquisition, targeting, interference, or task-effect mechanism is supported. Describe the commanded change and the visible residual state. Boundary. This code requires demonstrably unachieved local goal; an intentionally incremental movement or truncated, unobservable result may instead be partial/unconfirmed or unverifiable. Rejected commands are not executed-action M5 failures. Do not infer why the mechanism failed to move. Example. The note requests opening the gripper and releasing the object, but the fingers remain closed and the object remains clamped at the supported endpoint. M6 Unresolved mechanism. Definition. The local goal fails, but the available evidence does not identify more specific mechanism. Explanation. Use when the current local goal is demonstrably not achieved but the available evidence does not identify more specific action mechanism. State the failed local result, identify the missing or occluded evidence, and avoid choosing visually unsupported mechanical explanation. Boundary. M6 is different from an unverifiable outcome: failure itself must be supported. If non-retention is established but its contact geometry is unclear, use M1/S12 rather than M6. missing original note is not by itself evidence of failed local goal. Example. 26 The visible local target state is unchanged after an intended manipulation, but the relevant interaction is occluded and the evidence cannot distinguish incomplete motion from failed task effect. M7 Wrong local choice. Definition. The stated local selection or relation itself is unsuccessful; separate task mismatch is not sufficient. Explanation. Use when the call fails its own stated selection, ordering, or categorical-relation goal. The identifying issue is which object, answer, or relation was enacted, even if the low-level movement completed normally. The original local note and the relevant reference must support that discrepancy. Boundary. mismatch with the overall task is not sufficient if the action faithfully executes its own note; this does not by itself establish failed local action. Distinguish choosing the wrong named target from continuous targeting miss (M2). M7 remains unassessed in the preserved RoboDojo-Precision baseline. Example. The note requests pressing the key labeled 3, but the robot presses the clearly labeled 7 key. If the note itself requests 7 and the robot presses 7, that is not M7 merely because the overall task required 3. S1 Jaws close above object. Fingers close over the top rather than around the body; vertical miss must be visible. S2 Jaws close beside / ahead / behind. The object is outside the opposing jaw gap; record the visible lateral or depth offset. S3 Only rim / tip / edge pinched. Only shallow rim, tip, edge, or tapered surface is caught; name the contact region. S4 Closure pushes / tips object away. The acquiring hand pushes, rolls, or tips the object instead of enclosing it. S5 Support / another object caught. rest, fixture, support, or other object is caught instead of the intended target. S6 Receiving hand misses transfer. The receiving jaws fail to secure the transferred object; donor timing is not assumed. S7 Slip during initial lift. After transient capture, the object separates during the first lift; it did leave its support. S8 Slip during carry / wrist turn.
